title: Deep Dive: A Category Leader Goes On Sale
snippet: Investing in a >70% gross margin business priced for zero growth
content_html:
Every once in a while, the market prices a quality business as if it has been disrupted. The usual cause of this is weak results for 2-4 quarters followed by management pulling guidance.

There are many famous examples of this. In 2022, Meta at $88 was priced like a company that would never grow. Netflix in 2022 was similar. A few quarters of slowing subscriber growth were enough for the market to give up on it. Microsoft traded at a low-teens earnings multiple for 10 years before the cloud re-rating.

A quick highlight of why this happens. In recent years, there has been an explosion of quantamental pods. These use fundamental analysis coupled with quantitative metrics to invest in businesses. They focus exclusively on a few key metrics and improving those same metrics. They will sell at any price if their chosen metrics don’t improve. For example, if such a pod is invested in Netflix, it will trade at a 15x P/E ratio (or 10x P/E) if its metric weakens (e.g., subscriber growth declines from 10% to 8% YoY in a quarter). They are not long-term oriented and will stay in a business as long as their key metrics improve. So, if there are any signs of trouble, they will exit. This creates opportunities for investors like us, with a long-term orientation.

This setup pays twice: If growth returns, you gain from earnings growth and a multiple re-rating on top. A stock priced for no growth, moving towards being priced for modest growth, can re-rate materially with nothing heroic happening. The downside is protected as long as the business model remains intact. But the catch is that most cheap stocks deserve to be so. The key is to separate the broken franchises from those facing temporary air pockets.

We think we have found one such business. It is a category leader with >70% gross margins. It has recurring revenue, and customers use its products for years after their first use. The company has raised prices for a decade, and volumes have continued to grow, demonstrating its strong pricing power. It had no serious competition in its category for over a decade.

Then, about 2 years ago, several things went wrong. The flagship product got its first credible competitor in a decade. The product that was supposed to become the next billion-dollar franchise ran into a safety controversy. Traffic for their products rolled over, and volume growth flatlined. Management cut guidance twice and appeared to be sleeping at the wheel. The stock is now at the same price as it was 8 years ago.

According to our analysis, the current stock price prices in little or no cash flow growth over the next 5-10 years. For a business with strong margins (clear proof of pricing power) operating in a growing industry (with secular tailwinds), this seems like an overreaction to the headwinds it has faced over the last 2 years. The business has challenges, but the price already incorporates them, and we are getting paid well to take on this risk.
